Entry "~nai de" · pp. 271–273

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Making Requests · 「～ください」

N5 Grammar

～ている (Doing now)

Polite～ています
Casual～ている・～てる てる: spoken, everyday

Same meaning: "is doing". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

今いま、私わたしは緑茶りょくちゃを飲のんでいます。

"I'm drinking green tea right now."

ている after a verb means it's going on right now: not "I drink", but "I'm drinking".

It goes on the て-form: 飲む → 飲んで → 飲んでいる. On this card, it answers "what are you doing?".

ています is polite. Casual is ている, and in speech the い usually drops: 飲んでる.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 2

カフェやってる、白熊しろくまくんってかっこよくない？

"Isn't Shirokuma, the guy running the café, cool?"

やる → やって → やってる: ている with the い dropped. It also works for things you do these days, like running a café.

Examples

Your friend calls and asks what you're up to.

今いま、ご飯はんを食たべてる。

"I'm eating right now."

食べる → 食べて → 食べてる.

Casual

Looking out the window.

雨あめが降ふっていますね。

"It's raining, huh."

降る → 降って.

Polite

Your mom asks where your brother is.

部屋へやで寝ねてるよ。

"He's sleeping in his room."

寝る → 寝て.

Casual

Someone asks about your job these days.

銀行ぎんこうで働はたらいています。

"I work at a bank."

For things you do these days, too.

Polite

With and without

Without

今いま、本ほんを読よみます。

"I'll read a book now." About to start.

With ている

今いま、本ほんを読よんでいます。

"I'm reading a book now." Already in the middle of it.

Polite

YouTube · video

だから、今いま早はやく荷造にづくりをしています。

"So I'm packing fast right now."

する → して → しています.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 12

日夜にちや、パンダの世話せわを頑張がんばっています。

"He works hard looking after the pandas day and night."

頑張る → 頑張って. Something going on these days.

Polite

YouTube · video

音声おんせいは、今いま全部ぜんぶね、オートで撮影さつえいしています。

"The sound is all being recorded on auto right now."

撮影する (to film) → しています.

Polite

YouTube · video

湯気ゆげが出でています！

"It's steaming!"

出る → 出て.

Casual

Shashingo

小ちいさな家いえに、提灯ちょうちんがゆらゆらと揺ゆれている。

"A lantern is swaying by the little house."

揺れる (to sway) → 揺れて.

Casual

Source unknown No source

パラパラ降ふってる。

"It's drizzling."

降る → 降って → 降ってる.

Casual

Source unknown No source

イラレで描えがいてる？

"Are you drawing in Illustrator?"

描く → 描いて → 描いてる. イラレ is short for Illustrator.

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Other uses of the te-form · Using 「～ている」 for enduring states

N5 Grammar

～ている (State)

Polite～ています
Casual～ている・～てる てる: spoken, everyday

Same meaning: a state that lasts. Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

今いまは岡崎おかざきに地元じもとがあるんですけど、今いまは名古屋なごやに住すんでいます。

"My hometown is Okazaki, but now I live in Nagoya."

With some verbs, ている isn't an action going on. It's a state that lasts: 住む is moving in, 住んでいる is living there now.

Same shape as "is doing": 住む → 住んで → 住んでいる. The common ones: 住んでいる (live), 持っている (have), 知っている (know), 結婚している (married), 着ている (wearing).

ています is polite. Casual is ている, and in speech the い usually drops: 住んでる.

Casual

YouTube · video

やべ、やべえ。マシンガン持もってる。

"Oh no, oh no. They've got a machine gun." [playing a video game]

持つ is the moment you pick it up. 持ってる is having it now.

Examples

A coworker asks about your family.

姉あねは結婚けっこんしています。

"My older sister is married."

結婚する is the wedding day. 結婚している is being married.

Polite

Your friend mentions a café.

あ、その店みせ、知しってる！

"Oh, I know that place!"

知る is finding out. 知っている is knowing.

Casual

Pointing someone out at a party.

あの赤あかいセーターを着きている人ひとです。

"The person in the red sweater."

着る is putting it on. 着ている is wearing it.

Polite

Your friend looks worn out.

疲つかれてるね。

"You look tired."

疲れる is getting tired. 疲れている is being tired.

Casual

With and without

Without

大阪おおさかに住すみます。

"I'll live in Osaka." The move, not yet happened.

With ている

大阪おおさかに住すんでいます。

"I live in Osaka." You're there now.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

パーカーを着きていますねー。

"He's wearing a hoodie."

着る → 着て.

Polite

YouTube · My Five Favorite Things

新あたらしいキンドルは、防水ぼうすい機能きのうが付ついています。

"The new Kindle is waterproof."

付く (to come with) → 付いて: "it has".

Polite

Quartet · Episode 6

結婚けっこんしてるんですね

"You're married, aren't you?"

結婚している, shortened to してる: not the wedding itself, the state of being married.

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 9

もう何なにも残のこっていません

"There's nothing left."

残る ("remain") + ている: the state now. Negative: ていません.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

僕ぼくら、コウテイペンギンは、慣なれてるからいいけど…

"We emperor penguins are used to it, so we're fine, but..."

慣れる (to get used to) → 慣れてる: being used to it.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

なんだか、あちこち、ボロボロで汚よごれてるし

"It's kind of worn out and dirty all over."

汚れる (to get dirty) → 汚れてる: being dirty.

Casual

He Who Can't Marry · Episode 1

ちょっと冷ひえてるな。

"It's a bit cold."

冷える (to get cold) → 冷えてる.

Casual

Source unknown No source

皆みなさん、東京とうきょうの中なかにある秋葉原あきはばらっていう場所ばしょ知しってるかな？

"Everyone, do you know a place in Tokyo called Akihabara?"

知る → 知ってる: knowing.

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Other uses of the te-form · Enduring state-of-being vs enduring state of action

N5 Grammar

～ている (Habit)

Polite～ています
Casual～ている・～てる てる: spoken, everyday

Same meaning: "do regularly". Only the politeness changes.

～ている also talks about habits: things you do again and again, as part of your life right now. 毎朝走っている = "I run every morning".

It's the verb's て-form + いる: 走る → 走って → 走っている. Words like 毎日, 毎朝, いつも or 週に2回 make it clear it's a habit and not something happening right now.

Polite

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 10

毎日まいにち、自分じぶんと戦たたかっています。

"Every day, I fight with myself."

毎日 makes it a habit, and ています keeps it polite. On this card, it's something she does again and again, not just right now.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 3

ああやって いつも声こえ掛かけてるの

"[He] always calls out to people like that."

いつも points to a habit, and てる is the spoken ている. On this card, の at the end softly explains.

Examples

A coworker asks how you wake up so easily.

毎朝まいあさコーヒーを飲のんでいます。

"I drink coffee every morning."

Verbs whose て-form ends in で take でいる: 飲んで → 飲んでいる.

Polite

Someone asks if you do any sports.

週しゅうに3回かいジムに通かよっています。

"I go to the gym three times a week."

通う: to go somewhere regularly (school, gym, work).

Polite

A friend asks why you look so tired lately.

最近さいきん、毎晩まいばんゲームしてるんだ。

"I've been gaming every night lately."

Casual

A friend admires the bread you brought.

いつもこの店みせで買かってるよ。

"I always buy it at this shop."

Casual

With and without

Without

今朝けさ、走はしりました。

"I ran this morning." It happened once.

With ている

毎朝まいあさ、走はしっています。

"I run every morning." It's part of your routine.

毎日 + 通っている: a daily routine. 塾: cram school.

"I write a diary on my blog every day."

書いてる = 書いている. Polite because of んです at the end.

Polite

"I work part-time at the zoo two days a week."

週に２日: "two days a week". バイト: part-time job.

N5 Grammar

まだ～ていない

Politeまだ～ていません
Casualまだ～ていない・～てない てない: spoken, everyday

Same meaning: "haven't done it yet". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Good Morning Call · Episode 1

原因げんいんは まだ分わかっていません

"The cause still isn't known."

まだ + ていません says something hasn't happened yet, and it still might. It's the verb's て-form + いません.

On this card, 分かる → 分かって → 分かっていません, "isn't known yet".

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 2

まだ決きまってない。

"It's not decided yet."

Casual speech uses ていない, and the い often drops: ていない → てない. On this card, 決まる → 決まって → 決まってない.

Examples

Your friend asks if you've seen the new movie.

ううん、まだ見みてない。

"No, I haven't seen it yet."

Not 見なかった ("didn't watch"). まだ見ていない means you still might.

Casual

Your boss asks about the report.

すみません、まだ終おわっていません。

"Sorry, I haven't finished it yet."

終わる → 終わって.

Polite

Someone asks if you've eaten.

まだ食たべてないよ。一緒いっしょに行いく？

"I haven't eaten yet. Want to go together?"

食べる → 食べて.

Casual

At the station, a friend is late.

田中たなかさんはまだ来きていません。

"Tanaka hasn't come yet."

来る → 来て.

Polite

With and without

Without

昼ひるご飯はんを食たべなかった。

"I didn't eat lunch." That's over, you skipped it.

With まだ～ていない

まだ昼ひるご飯はんを食たべていない。

"I haven't eaten lunch yet." You still plan to.

Sentence mining

Polite

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 7

まだ部屋へやは 決きまってないんですけどね。

"I haven't decided on a place yet, though."

まだ + 決まる ("be decided") → 決まってない = "not decided yet". んですけどね: "though".

Casual

Source unknown No source

で、まだ何なにも装備そうび持もってないので。

"Thing is, I don't have any gear yet, so..."

持つ → 持ってない: "don't have yet".

Casual

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 7

まだ何なにも決きまってないし。

"Nothing's been decided yet."

Casual speech drops the い: 決まっていない → 決まってない.

Casual

Million Yen Woman · Episode 1

あら、まだ慣なれてないの？

"Oh, you're still not used to it?"

まだ + 慣れる ("get used to") → 慣れてない = "still not used to it". あら: a soft "oh".

Casual

Border · Episode 1

まだ死しんでない。

"I'm not dead yet."

まだ + 死ぬ ("die") → 死んでない = "not dead yet".

Casual

Daily Lives of High School Boys · Episode 8

ああ、まだ見みてない。

"Oh, I haven't watched it yet."

まだ + 見る ("watch") → 見てない = "haven't watched it yet".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 33

まだ戦たたかいは終おわってないぞ。

"The battle isn't over yet."

Short for 終わっていない.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 18

まだ何なにも話はなしてないのに。

"I haven't even said anything yet."

Nothing has happened so far, but it could.

N5 Grammar

～てもいい

Polite～てもいいです(か)
Casual～てもいい・～ていい ていい: shorter, spoken

Same meaning: "it's okay to". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

YouTube · video

もうちょっと、感度かんど早はやくしてみてもいいかな。

"Maybe I can try making the sensitivity a bit faster." [changing a game setting]

てもいい after a verb means it's okay to do it: allowed, or fine.

It goes on the て-form: してみる (try) → してみて + もいい. On this card, かな makes it "maybe I could...".

To ask for permission, add か: てもいいですか is polite, てもいい？ is casual.

Polite

Border · Episode 6

座すわってもいいですか？

"May I sit down?"

てもいいです is polite "it's okay to", and か turns it into asking for permission. On this card, 座る → 座って → 座ってもいいですか.

Examples

In a shop, you want to try on a jacket.

着きてもいいですか？

"Can I try it on?"

着る ("put on") → 着て + もいいですか = "may I put it on?", "can I try it on?".

Polite

At your friend's place, you're thirsty.

これ、飲のんでもいい？

"Can I drink this?"

飲む ("drink") → 飲んで + もいい = "is it okay to drink?". Casual: no ですか.

Casual

The teacher before the test.

辞書じしょを使つかってもいいですよ。

"You can use a dictionary."

使う ("use") → 使って + もいいです = "you may use it". よ: telling them it's allowed.

Polite

Your friend looks tired.

もう帰かえっていいよ。

"You can go home now."

帰る ("go home") → 帰って + いい = "you can go home". In speech the も often drops.

Casual

With and without

Without

写真しゃしんを撮とりますか？

"Will you take a photo?" Just asking what someone will do.

With てもいい

写真しゃしんを撮とってもいいですか？

"May I take a photo?" Asking if it's allowed.

Source unknown No source

"Is it okay if I film just your hands?"

撮っている → 撮ってて: "be filming".

Polite

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 3

ひとつ聞きいてもいいですか？

"Can I ask you something?"

聞く ("ask") → 聞いて + もいいですか = "may I ask?". ひとつ: "one thing".

Casual

YouTube · video

あ、でもリチウムとか取とりに行いってもいいかもしれんな。

"Oh, but maybe I could go get some lithium."

行く → 行って. かもしれん is a casual "maybe".

Casual

Source unknown No source

だからさ、仕事しごと、辞やめて、専業せんぎょう主婦しゅふしていいよ。

"So you can quit your job and be a homemaker."

する → して. ていい is the short form.

Casual

Source unknown No source

そんなに飛とばして大丈夫だいじょうぶ？

"Is it okay to go that fast?"

て大丈夫 works like てもいい: "is it fine to".

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 3

見みててもいい？

"Can I keep looking?"

見ている ("be watching") → 見てて + もいい = "may I keep watching?".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 20

一緒いっしょに行いってもいい？

"Can I go with you?"

Asking permission: て-form + もいい.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 36

豆腐とうふ入いれていい？

"Can I put the tofu in?"

Casual speech can drop the も.

N5 Grammar

～てはいけない・
～ちゃいけない

Polite～てはいけません
Casual～てはいけない firm, rules
～ちゃいけない same, said faster
～ちゃだめ spoken, softer

Same meaning: "you must not". Only the politeness changes. In speech, ～ては becomes ～ちゃ, and ～では becomes ～じゃ.

Polite

Mob Psycho 100 · Episode 5

人ひとに向むけてはいけません

"You must not point it at people."

To say something isn't allowed, use the verb's て-form + はいけません. It's firm, like a rule.

On this card, 向ける ("point") → 向けて → 向けてはいけません.

Casual

Quartet · Episode 7

見みちゃダメ

"Don't look."

In speech ては becomes ちゃ, and だめ is softer than いけない. On this card, 見ては → 見ちゃ + ダメ.

Examples

A sign in the library.

ここで食たべてはいけません。

"No eating here."

食べる → 食べて + はいけません.

Polite

A parent to a kid by the road.

一人ひとりで行おこなっちゃだめよ。

"You can't go on your own."

行って + は → 行っちゃ. だめ = no good.

Casual

The teacher before the test.

辞書じしょを使つかってはいけません。

"You may not use a dictionary."

使う → 使って.

Polite

Your friend is about to open your present early.

まだ開あけちゃだめ！

"Don't open it yet!"

開けて + は → 開けちゃ.

Casual

Your little brother reaches for the hot pan.

それ、触さわっちゃいけないよ。

"You can't touch that."

触って + は → 触っちゃ. Same as 触ってはいけない, just said faster.

Casual

Hiking with a friend, who bends down to a stream.

この水みずは飲のんじゃいけないよ。

"You can't drink this water."

飲んで + は → 飲んじゃ. The て-form ends in で, so you get じゃ, not ちゃ.

Casual

With and without

Without

写真しゃしんを撮とってもいいです。

"You may take photos." Allowed.

With てはいけない

写真しゃしんを撮とってはいけません。

"You must not take photos." Not allowed.

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 5

混乱こんらんしてはいけませんので

"...so there's no confusion."

Polite: てはいけません. Here with ので, giving the reason.

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 11

諦あきらめちゃダメですよ。

"You can't give up."

諦める ("give up") → 諦めて + は, said 諦めちゃ + ダメ = "you can't give up". ですよ keeps it polite.

Polite

ReLIFE · Episode 9

失敗しっぱいは 忘わすれてはいけないと思おもいます。

"I don't think I should forget my failure."

忘れる ("forget") → 忘れて + はいけない = "mustn't forget". と思います: "I think".

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 12

持もち込こんじゃいけません！

"You can't bring that in!"

Verbs ending in んで take じゃ.

Casual

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 4

余計よけいなものは見みてはいけない。

"Don't look at anything else."

見る ("look") → 見て + はいけない = "mustn't look". 余計なもの: "anything unnecessary".

Casual

Mob Psycho 100 · Episode 12

人ひとを傷きずつけてはいけないんだぞ。

"You mustn't hurt people."

傷つける ("hurt") → 傷つけて + はいけない = "mustn't hurt". んだぞ: said firmly, like a lesson.

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 2

動物どうぶつ飼かっちゃいけないの。

"We're not allowed to keep animals."

飼う ("keep a pet") → 飼って + は, said 飼っちゃ + いけない. の: explaining the situation.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 1

寝ねちゃダメよ。

"Don't fall asleep."

寝る ("sleep") → 寝ては, said 寝ちゃ + ダメ = "don't fall asleep".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 21

飼育しいく係かかりが自分じぶんで食たべちゃダメでしょ。

"A keeper can't go eating it themselves."

ダメ can take the place of いけない.

N5 Grammar

～なくてはいけない・～なきゃ

Polite～なくてはいけません also ～なければなりません: more formal
Casual～なくちゃ・～なきゃ spoken; いけない after it often drops

Same meaning: "have to, must". Only the politeness changes.

To say you have to do something, take the verb's ない-form, change the last い to くては, then add いけない: 行かない → 行かなくてはいけない, "I have to go". Literally: "not going won't do".

In everyday speech it gets squeezed: なくては → なくちゃ, なければ → なきゃ, and the いけない often drops: 行かなきゃ！

Polite

YouTube · video

3冊さつ、日本にほんに持もって帰かえらなければいけません。

"I have to take three books back to Japan."

なければいけません is a common polite way to say "have to". On this card, 持って帰る → 持って帰らない → 持って帰らなければいけません.

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 4

すぐお見舞みまい行いかなきゃ。

"I have to go visit [them] right away."

なきゃ is the squeezed なければ, and the いけない has dropped. On this card, 行かない → 行かなきゃ.

Examples

Leaving the office party early. Your boss asks why.

明日あしたは6時じに起おきなくてはいけません。

"I have to get up at six tomorrow."

Polite

The doctor hands over a prescription.

この薬くすりは毎日まいにち飲のまなければなりません。

"You must take this medicine every day."

なければなりません: the formal version, for rules and official talk.

Polite

You check the time at a friend's place.

あ、もう帰かえらなきゃ。

"Oh, I have to go home."

Casual

Sunday evening, your kid is still playing.

宿題しゅくだい、やらなくちゃね。

"You've got to do your homework, right?"

Casual

With and without

Without

明日あしたは早はやく起おきる。

"I'll get up early tomorrow." Just a plan.

With なきゃ

明日あしたは早はやく起おきなきゃ。

"I have to get up early tomorrow." No choice.

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 2

近ちかいうちに 話はなさなきゃいけないと思おもってます

"I think I have to tell them soon."

話さない → 話さなきゃいけない. 近いうちに: "one of these days, soon".

Polite

Sailor Suit and Machine Gun · Episode 4

組長くみちょうは僕ぼくが 助たすけなきゃいけないんです！

"I'm the one who has to save the boss!"

助けない → 助けなきゃいけない.

Casual

"I need to get my rain boots out."

なきゃ alone, いけない dropped.

Casual

Border · Episode 9

絶対ぜったい的てきな正義せいぎに ならなくてはいけない

"You have to become absolute justice."

The full form: ならない → ならなくてはいけない.

Casual

Weakest Beast · Episode 8

社員しゃいん 養やしなわなきゃいけない

"I have staff to feed."

養う: to support, feed (a family, staff).

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 1

いずれ 私わたしが 介護かいごしなきゃいけないんだし

"Sooner or later I'll have to look after them."

介護する: to care for (the old or sick). いずれ: "sooner or later".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 40

家出いえで、止とめなくちゃ。

"We have to stop this running away from home."

なくちゃ is the short なくてはいけない.

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 45

ほら、寝ねてなきゃダメよ。

"Come on, you have to stay in bed."

なきゃ is the shortest form.

N5 Grammar

～てから

Polite

YouTube · video

こんなに朝あさ早はやく起おきるようになったのは、子供こどもが生うまれてからですね。

"I started getting up this early after my kid was born."

てから after a verb means after doing it: first one thing, then the rest.

It goes on the て-form: 生まれる → 生まれて + から. On this card, it answers "since when?" or "after what?": since the baby was born.

The politeness sits at the end of the sentence, not on てから. Plain ～て only says "and"; てから makes the order clear.

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 5

帰かえってからずっと勉強べんきょうしてるの。

"He's been studying ever since he got home."

てから means "after" or "since". On this card, 帰る ("get home") → 帰って + から = "since getting home", and ずっと勉強してる = "has been studying the whole time".

Examples

Your friend wants to go out right now.

宿題しゅくだいをしてから行いくね。

"I'll go after I do my homework."

する → して.

Casual

At the table, a kid grabs the food.

手てを洗あらってから食たべてください。

"Please wash your hands before you eat."

Literally "after washing your hands, eat".

Polite

Someone asks how long you've been in Japan.

日本にほんに来きてから、三さん年ねんです。

"It's been three years since I came to Japan."

来る → 来て.

Polite

Planning the evening with a friend.

ご飯はんを食たべてから、映画えいがを見みよう。

"Let's watch a movie after we eat."

食べる → 食べて.

Casual

With and without

Without

ご飯はんを食たべて、映画えいがを見みます。

"I eat and watch a movie." Just two things in a row.

With てから

ご飯はんを食たべてから、映画えいがを見みます。

"I watch a movie after I eat." The eating comes first, for sure.

Polite

Source unknown No source

マヨネーズは、じゃがいもが冷さめてから、入いれましょう。

"Add the mayo after the potatoes cool down."

冷める (to cool down) → 冷めて.

Casual

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 1

じゃ、帰かえってから ケーキ食たべなさいよ。

"Then have some cake when you get home."

帰る ("get home") → 帰って + から = "after you get home". Then ケーキ食べなさい: "eat the cake".

Casual

The Journalist · Episode 1

それを終おわらせてから 名古屋なごやに入はいって

"After I finish that, I'll go to Nagoya..."

終わらせる ("finish") → 終わらせて + から = "after finishing that". Then 名古屋に入る: "go into Nagoya".

Casual

Bunny Drop · Episode 7

パパは お仕事しごと 終おわってから来くるの。

"Papa's coming after work."

終わる ("end") → 終わって + から = "after work ends". Then 来る: "he'll come".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 37

お店みせ終おわってからでいいから。

"After you close the shop is fine."

終わる ("close, end") → 終わって + から + でいい = "after you close is fine".

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 1

母親ははおやが死しんでから

"Since their mother died…"

死ぬ → 死んで + から: "since she died". When the て-form ends in で, it's でから.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 26

ご飯はん食たべてからにするよ。

"I'll do it after I eat."

Eat first, then the other thing.

N5 Grammar

ほしい (欲しい)

Polite欲しいです
Casual欲しい

Same meaning: "want". Only the politeness changes.

Casual

YouTube · video

普通ふつうの工具こうぐ箱ばこが、欲ほしいんだよな。

"I just want a normal toolbox."

欲しい means want, for a thing: a toolbox, a coffee, new shoes. The thing you want takes が: 工具箱が欲しい.

On this card, it answers "What do you want?": a normal toolbox. んだよな adds "that's the thing, you know".

Add です to make it polite: 欲しいです. For an action, use たい instead: 買いたい (want to buy).

Polite

Border · Episode 9

欲ほしいです

"I want it."

欲しい + です is the polite form. On this card, the boy says just that, about the thing in front of him.

Examples

Your birthday is coming up. A friend asks.

新あたらしいスマホが欲ほしいな。

"I want a new phone."

な = thinking out loud.

Casual

At a café, to the staff.

お水みずが欲ほしいんですが。

"Could I get some water?"

んですが turns it into a soft request.

Polite

Shopping with a friend.

何なにが欲ほしい？

"What do you want?"

Casual

A busy week. A coworker asks how you are.

ちょっと休やすみが欲ほしいです。

"I could use a little break."

Polite

Someone offers you their old stuff.

そんなもの、欲ほしくないよ。

"I don't want that kind of thing."

It works like an い-adjective: 欲しい → 欲しくない.

Casual

With and without

Without

コーヒーを飲のむ。

"I'm having a coffee." Just what I do.

With 欲しい

コーヒーが欲ほしい。

"I want a coffee." What I wish I had.

Sentence mining

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 11

欲ほしいもの ないですか？

"Is there anything you want?"

欲しい ("want") + もの ("thing") = "a thing you want". ないですか: "isn't there?".

Casual

YouTube · video

で、ショットガン自体じたいは、ま、作つくれそうなんですけど、どうせだったらライフルが欲ほしいのよね。

"I could probably make the shotgun, but if I'm at it, I want a rifle."

Casual

Source unknown No source

切実せつじつに鉄てつが欲ほしいのに、鉄てつがどこにもないよ。

"I really need iron, but there's none anywhere."

Casual

Source unknown No source

いくらでも欲ほしいもんがあるけれども。

"There's no end of stuff I want, though."

欲しい ("want") + もん (casual もの, "stuff") = "stuff I want". いくらでも: "no end of".

Casual

Source unknown No source

何なにが、序盤じょばん1番ばん欲ほしいかな。

"What do I want most early on?"

Casual

Source unknown No source

リアルはいいの、夢ゆめが欲ほしいのね？

"Forget reality, I want dreams, okay?"

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 35

私わたしは手袋てぶくろが欲ほしいのよ。

"I want gloves."

The thing you want takes が.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 13

お嫁よめさんが欲ほしい。

"I want a wife."

Written on a wish card.

Entry "hoshii¹" · pp. 144–146

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Desire and Suggestions · Using 「欲しい」

N5 Grammar

～たい

Polite～たいです
Casual～たい

Same meaning: "want to". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

今日きょうは、ちょっと仮眠かみんを取とりたいですね。

"Today I'd like to grab a quick nap." [tired after traveling]

たい means want to: it's about an action you want to do, not a thing you want.

Take the ます form and swap ます for たい: 取ります → 取りたい. On this card, it answers "what do you feel like doing?": a nap.

Add です to make it polite: 取りたいです.

Casual

YouTube · video

じゃあ、宝たからくじが当あたったら何なにをしたい？

"So, if you won the lottery, what would you want to do?"

Casual: just たい, no です. します → したい. "Don't want to" works like an い-adjective: たい → たくない.

Examples

It's 35 degrees out. You and a friend are walking past the beach.

海うみで泳およぎたいなあ。

"I want to go swimming in the sea."

泳ぎます → 泳ぎたい. なあ = thinking out loud.

Casual

A shop clerk asks if you need help. You point at a jacket.

これ、着きてみたいんですが。

"I'd like to try this on."

着てみます → 着てみたい. んですが makes it a soft request.

Polite

Your friend wants to go out. You're exhausted.

今日きょうはどこも行いきたくない。

"I don't want to go anywhere today."

行きたい → 行きたくない. Same as い-adjectives: い → くない.

Casual

A coworker asks about your plans for the holidays.

京都きょうとに行いきたいです。

"I'd like to go to Kyoto."

行きます → 行きたい + です.

Polite

With and without

Without

ラーメンを食たべます。

"I'm going to eat ramen." Just what you'll do.

With たい

ラーメンを食たべたいです。

"I want to eat ramen." What you feel like doing.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

ちょっとあの、大だい音量おんりょうにはしたくないんですよね。

"I don't really want to turn the volume way up."

したい → したくない. んです makes it polite here, no です after たくない needed.

Polite

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 8

力ちからになりたいんです。

"I want to help you."

なる → なりたい. んです makes it polite.

Polite

Smoking · Episode 8

はい　行いきたいです！

"Yes, I want to go!"

行きます → 行きたい + です.

Casual

YouTube · video

狼おおかみがうろうろしてるので、近ちかづきたくない。

"There are wolves wandering around, so I don't want to get close."

近づきたい → 近づきたくない.

Casual

YouTube · video

人ひとの少すくない場所ばしょに行いきたい、そうして、僕ぼくは電車でんしゃに乗のりました。

"'I want to go somewhere with fewer people.' And so I got on the train."

The thought itself is casual: 行きたい. The narration after it is polite.

Casual

Weakest Beast · Episode 5

海うみが見みたい。

"I want to see the sea."

見る ("see") → 見たい = "want to see". 海 ("the sea") + が: with たい, が often replaces を.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 2

帰かえりたいよ。

"I want to go home."

帰ります drops ます, adds たい.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 36

何なに食たべたい？

"What do you want to eat?"

A plain question with no か.

N5 Grammar

～ませんか

Polite～ませんか
Casual～ない？ ない form, voice goes up

Same meaning: "won't you, want to?". Only the politeness changes.

ませんか is how you invite someone: "would you like to...?", "why don't we...?". Swap ます for ませんか: 行きます → 行きませんか.

Literally it's "won't you go?". Asking it the negative way is softer: it's easy for the other person to say no.

Casual: the ない form with a rising voice: 行かない？

Polite

Legal High · Episode 7

そうだ。 温泉おんせん 入はいりませんか？

"I know! Why don't we get in the hot spring?"

ませんか invites someone: swap ます for ませんか. On this card, 入ります → 入りませんか.

Casual

Good Morning Call · Season 2, Episode 8

一緒いっしょに行いかない？

"Want to go together?"

The ない form with a rising voice is the casual invitation. On this card, 行かない？ sounds like "you're not going?" but means "want to go?".

Examples

Inviting a coworker.

一緒いっしょに昼ひるご飯はんを食たべませんか。

"Would you like to have lunch together?"

食べます → 食べませんか.

Polite

Texting a friend.

週末しゅうまつ、映画えいが見みない？

"Want to watch a movie this weekend?"

Casual: the ない form, voice up at the end.

Casual

Talking to a neighbor.

今度こんど、うちに来きませんか。

"Why don't you come over sometime?"

Polite

A hot day, walking with a friend.

ちょっと休やすまない？

"Want to take a break?"

休む → 休まない.

Casual

With and without

Without

映画えいがを見みますか。

"Are you watching a movie?" A plain question, just asking.

With ませんか

映画えいがを見みませんか。

"Would you like to watch a movie?" An invitation, usually with me.

N5 Grammar

～ましょう

Polite～ましょう
Casual～よう る-verbs: drop る
～おう う-verbs: u sound → o

Same meaning: "let's". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

今日きょうは、一緒いっしょにこの博多はかたの夜よるの街まちを歩あるきましょう！

"Today, let's walk around Hakata at night together!" [to her viewers]

ましょう means let's: you suggest doing something, and you're doing it too.

Take the ます form and swap ます for ましょう: 歩きます → 歩きましょう. On this card, it answers "what are we doing?": she's taking us along on her walk.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 14

次つぎはかき氷ごおり食たべよう。

"Next, let's have shaved ice."

Casual: る-verbs swap る for よう (食べる → 食べよう). う-verbs turn the last u sound into o and add う (行く → 行こう). する → しよう, 来る → こよう.

Examples

You and a friend walk past a ramen shop, both starving.

ラーメン食たべよう！

"Let's get ramen!"

食べる is a る-verb: る → よう.

Casual

A meeting runs late. You look at your coworkers.

そろそろ帰かえりましょう。

"Let's call it a day."

帰ります → 帰りましょう. そろそろ = "about time".

Polite

It starts pouring and the station is far.

タクシーで帰かえろう。

"Let's take a taxi home."

帰る is a う-verb, so the last sound る (ru) turns into ろ (ro) + う.

Casual

The teacher walks into class.

じゃあ、始はじめましょう。

"Okay, let's begin."

始めます → 始めましょう.

Polite

Halfway up a hill, your friend is out of breath.

ちょっと休やすもう。

"Let's rest a bit."

休む → む (mu) turns into も (mo) + う.

Casual

With and without

Without

公園こうえんに行いきます。

"I'm going to the park." Just telling them your plan.

With ましょう

公園こうえんに行いきましょう。

"Let's go to the park." You're inviting them to come along.

N5 Grammar

～ましょうか

Polite～ましょうか
Casual～ようか る-verbs: drop る
～おうか う-verbs: u sound → o

Same meaning: "shall I, shall we". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

お箸はし、お付つけしましょうか？

"Would you like chopsticks?" [at the register]

ましょうか means shall I or shall we: you offer to do something, or suggest doing it together.

Swap ます for ましょうか. On this card, it's the extra polite shop version: お付けします (I'll add some) → お付けしましょうか. It answers "Do you want this?" before the customer has to ask.

Casual: the よう form + か: 付けようか, 持とうか. Without か, ましょう is just "let's".

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 2

そうしようか

"Shall we do that?"

The casual form is the よう form + か. On this card, する → しよう → しようか, and そう means "that way".

Examples

A coworker is carrying a heavy box.

持もちましょうか。

"Shall I carry that?"

持ちます → 持ちましょうか.

Polite

Your friend looks cold.

窓まど、閉しめようか？

"Want me to close the window?"

Casual: 閉める → 閉めよう + か.

Casual

It's getting late at a meeting.

じゃあ、帰かえりましょうか。

"Well, shall we head home?"

Polite

Planning dinner with a friend.

何なに食たべようか。

"What should we eat?"

With a question word: "what shall we...?"

Casual

With and without

Without

窓まどを閉しめましょう。

"Let's close the window." A suggestion, already decided.

With ましょうか

窓まどを閉しめましょうか。

"Shall I close the window?" An offer: you ask first.

N5 Grammar

でも (Or something)

Casual

Pokémon The Series: Indigo League · Episode 2

何なんとかするよ弁償べんしょうでも何なんでも。

"I'll sort it out. Pay you back [for the bike] or whatever."

でも goes right after a noun and means "or something". It takes the place of を or が.

On this card, the noun becomes just an example: paying back is one idea, but he'll do anything. 何でも adds "or anything at all".

Same in polite and casual speech. You hear it most in suggestions and invitations, often with ～ませんか or ～ましょうか.

Polite

Demon Slayer - Kimetsu no Yaiba · Episode 24

お茶ちゃでもどうですか～？

"How about some tea?"

でも after a noun softens it to "... or something". On this card, お茶 ("tea") + でも + どうですか ("how about?") is a soft invitation: it doesn't have to be tea.

Examples

You and a friend have 30 minutes before the movie.

コーヒーでも飲のむ？

"Want to get a coffee or something?"

Casual

A coworker looks tired after a long meeting.

お茶ちゃでも飲のみませんか。

"Shall we have some tea or something?"

Polite

It's Sunday and you're both bored.

映画えいがでも見みに行いこうか。

"Should we go see a movie or something?"

Casual

A guest arrives early and has to wait.

ここで雑誌ざっしでも読よんでいてください。

"Please read a magazine or something here [while you wait]."

Polite

With and without

Without

コーヒーを飲のむ？

"Do you want to drink coffee?" A question about coffee, specifically.

With でも

コーヒーでも飲のむ？

"Want to get a coffee or something?" Coffee is just an example. It sounds relaxed, and your friend can easily say "let's get tea instead."

Not the same as the でも that means "but". That one starts a new sentence (でも、高い). This one sits right after a noun, inside the sentence (お茶でも飲む).

N5 Grammar

～つもりだ

Polite～つもりです
Casual～つもりだ plain statement
～つもり just the word, very common

Same meaning: "plan to". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

Last Samurai Standing · Episode 1

また、刀かたなを抜ぬくおつもりですか？

"Are you planning to draw your sword again?"

つもり means plan to, intend to: something you've already decided to do.

It goes right after the dictionary form: 抜く + つもり. On this card, it answers "what have you made up your mind to do?": draw the sword.

Add です to make it polite. Here it's asked about someone else, so お is added on top: おつもりですか.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 14

ペン子こさんにアタックするつもりで

"With the plan of making a move on Penko-san..."

Casual: つもり on its own, or つもりだ. Here it's つもりで, "with that plan in mind", and the sentence carries on.

Examples

A friend asks what you're doing this weekend. You've already booked the tickets.

土曜どよう日ひに映画えいがを見みるつもり。

"I'm planning to see a movie on Saturday."

見る + つもり. Already decided, not just a wish.

Casual

Your boss asks about your plans after the contract ends.

来年らいねん、日本にほんに引ひっ越こすつもりです。

"I'm planning to move to Japan next year."

引っ越す + つもり + です.

Polite

Your friend thinks you'll go to the party. You won't.

今日きょうは行いかないつもり。

"I'm not planning to go today."

For "plan not to", put the verb in ない form: 行かない + つもり.

Casual

A coworker sees you packing up early.

今日きょうは早はやく帰かえるつもりです。

"I'm planning to go home early today."

帰る + つもり + です.

Polite

With and without

Without

京都きょうとに行いきたいです。

"I want to go to Kyoto." Just a wish, maybe one day.

With つもり

京都きょうとに行いくつもりです。

"I'm planning to go to Kyoto." You've decided.

その ("that") + つもり ("plan, intention") + です = "that's my plan". 就職したら: "once I get a job".

N5 Grammar

もらう (貰う)

Polite

YouTube · video

お水みずってもらえますか?

"Could I get some water?" [to the staff at a restaurant]

もらう means to get, to receive: something comes to you from someone else.

The thing gets を (here って, casual for を), the giver gets に or から. On this card, もらえる is "can get", so もらえますか is "can I get?", the everyday way to ask for something.

Polite: もらいます, もらいました. Casual: もらう, もらった.

Casual

Death Note · Episode 12

いいヒントをもらった。

"You've given me a good clue."

もらう is receiving, told from the side of the person who gets it. On this card, もらった = "I received", and the giver doesn't need to be said.

Examples

A coworker asks about your new watch.

父ちちにもらいました。

"I got it from my dad."

The giver gets に: 父に. Who received? You, so no need to say it.

Polite

Your friend sees a pile of chocolate on your desk.

みんなからもらった。

"I got them from everyone."

から works too: "from everyone". に and から mean the same here.

Casual

At the hotel front desk, you want a map.

地図ちずをもらえますか。

"Could I get a map?"

The thing gets を: 地図を.

Polite

The shop is giving away free samples.

これ、もらっていい？

"Can I take this?"

もらっていい: "is it okay if I take it?"

Casual

With and without

Without

友達ともだちが本ほんをくれました。

"My friend gave me a book." The friend is the one doing it.

With もらう

友達ともだちに本ほんをもらいました。

"I got a book from my friend." Same event, but told from your side: you're the one receiving.

"I even got his autograph!"

サイン ("autograph") + も ("even") + もらいました ("got") = "I even got his autograph".

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Giving and Receiving · When to use 「もらう」

N5 Grammar

あげる

あげる means to give: something goes away from you (or the person the story is about) to someone else.

The thing gets を, the person who receives gets に: 友達に花をあげる, "give flowers to a friend". It never goes towards you: when someone gives something to you, that's くれる.

Polite: あげます, あげました. Casual: あげる, あげた.

Examples

A coworker asks what you did with your old bike.

弟おとうとにあげました。

"I gave it to my little brother."

The receiver gets に: 弟に. Who gave? You, so no need to say it.

Polite

Your friend admires your scarf. You don't wear it anymore.

それ、あげるよ。

"You can have it."

Literally "I'll give it (to you)". From you, to them: あげる.

Casual

It's Valentine's Day. Your friend is holding a box of chocolates.

誰だれにあげるの？

"Who are you giving them to?"

It also works for other people giving: here your friend gives, someone else gets.

Casual

At the park, a child asks if they can feed your dog.

犬いぬにパンをあげないでください。

"Please don't give the dog bread."

Feeding an animal is also あげる: 犬に + パンを.

Polite

With and without

Without

友達ともだちが本ほんをくれました。

"My friend gave me a book." The book comes to you.

With あげる

友達ともだちに本ほんをあげました。

"I gave my friend a book." The book goes away from you, to your friend.

あなたに ("to you") + 花を ("flowers") + あげましょう = "I'll give you flowers", a polite offer.

あげます ("I'll give") + よ = "you can have it". Who gets what is clear from the scene.

Advice can be "given" with あげる too.

あげよう + か makes it an offer.

N5 Grammar

くれる・てくれる

Polite

YouTube · video

今いまは、僕ぼくの妻つまのお母ははさんが、代かわりに世話せわをしてくれています。

"Right now, my wife's mom is looking after [it] for us instead."

くれる means someone gives to me (or to my side: my family, my friends). After a て-form it means someone does something for me.

On this card: 世話をして + くれる. It answers "who's helping us out?": my wife's mom.

Polite: くれます. Here it's くれています, "is doing it for us" right now.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 2

じゃ、白熊しろくま君くん、肩かた揉もんでくれる？

"Then, Polar Bear, will you massage my shoulders?"

Casual: plain くれる. Asked as a question, it's a friendly favor: "will you do this for me?"

Examples

Your friend just got back from Kyoto and handed you a box of sweets. You tell your sister.

友達ともだちがお土産みやげをくれた。

"My friend gave me a souvenir."

Plain くれる: the thing comes to me. No "me" needed, くれる already says it.

Casual

A coworker likes your new pen and asks where it's from.

これ、部長ぶちょうがくれました。

"My boss gave me this."

Only toward you or your side. When YOU give something, it's a different verb (あげる).

Polite

You missed the bus, but your mom drove you to the station.

母ははが駅えきまで送おくってくれました。

"My mom drove me to the station."

送って + くれる: she did it for me.

Polite

Your friend is about to leave, but you need one more minute.

ちょっと待まってくれる？

"Can you wait a sec?"

A question with くれる = asking a favor.

Casual

With and without

Without

友達ともだちが手伝てつだいました。

"My friend helped." Just a fact. Helped who? Not said.

With くれる

友達ともだちが手伝てつだってくれました。

"My friend helped me out." It was for me, and I'm glad.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

守まもり神がみの意味いみは、守まもってくれる神かみ様さまのことです。

"A 守り神 is a god who protects you."

守って + くれる: protects (us).

Polite

YouTube · video

はい。皆みなさん、本当ほんとうにいつも応援おうえんしてくれて、本当ほんとうにありがとうございます。

"Yes. Everyone, thank you so much for always supporting me."

～てくれてありがとう: thanks for doing it (for me).

Polite

Comprehensible Japanese · これ、それ、あれ、どれ

この動画どうがをみてくれて、ありがとうございます。

"Thank you for watching this video."

見て + くれて + ありがとう. You watched, for me.

Casual

Source unknown No source

なあ、そのおむすび、俺おれにもくれよ！

"Hey, give me one of those rice balls too!"

Plain くれる, "give me". くれ is the blunt command form.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 12

パンダのストラップもつけてくれるし

"And they even put a panda strap on it for you."

つけて + くれる: the shop does it for you.

Casual

YouTube · video

QRコードを、あの読よみ込こんだら、そうガイドしてくれる。

"If you scan the QR code, it guides you."

Even a machine can くれる: it does something for you.

Casual

Legal High · Episode 11

お前まえも 泣ないてくれるのか？

"You'll cry for me too?"

泣いて + くれる: someone does something for the speaker.

Casual

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 2

やめてくれよ

"Stop it, will you?"

くれ is the rough command form of くれる: "do me the favor of stopping".

N5 Grammar

そして・それから

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 8

そして、ある吹雪ふぶきの日ひ。

"And then, one snowy day..." [telling a story]

そして means and or and then, at the start of a sentence. It hooks what comes next onto what was just said.

On this card, it moves a story along: this happened, and then, one day in a snowstorm... It answers "What happened next?".

It's the same in polite and casual speech. You hear it a lot in stories and explanations; in chat people often say それから or で.

Polite

YouTube · video

それからシャンプーとかボディーソープとか、いろんなものがあります。

"And they also have shampoo, body soap, all kinds of stuff."

それから is "and then" or "and also": the next thing in time, or the next thing on a list. Here it adds more things to the list.

Examples

Telling a friend about your morning.

朝あさご飯はんを食たべました。それから、学校がっこうに行いきました。

"I had breakfast. Then I went to school."

それから = after that.

Polite

Introducing yourself.

私わたしは学生がくせいです。そして、カフェで働はたらいています。

"I'm a student. And I work at a café."

Polite

Telling a friend what to buy.

卵たまごと牛乳ぎゅうにゅう。それから、パンも。

"Eggs and milk. Oh, and bread too."

それから adds one more thing.

Casual

Describing your hotel room.

部屋へやは広ひろい。そして、すごく静しずか。

"The room is big. And really quiet."

Casual

With and without

Without

部屋へやは広ひろいです。静しずかです。

"The room is big. It's quiet." Two loose facts.

With そして

部屋へやは広ひろいです。そして、静しずかです。

"The room is big. And it's quiet." The second fact is added on.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

そして、すごくまぶしいです。

"And it's really bright."

Polite

NHK やさしいことばニュース · 暑い日が続く　熱中症に気をつけて

そして、のどが乾かわいていなくても、水みずを飲のんでください。

"And drink water even when you're not thirsty."

Polite

Source unknown No source

そして、また月曜げつよう日ひが始はじまります。

"And then Monday starts all over again."

Polite

Source unknown No source

そして、お水みずを一杯いっぱい飲のみました。

"And then I drank a glass of water."

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 8

そして 主人しゅじんと出会であいました

"And then I met my husband."

そして moves the story to the next step.

Casual

Source unknown No source

それから、買かい物もの行いって…

"Then go shopping..."

それから = "after that, then". 買い物行って: "go shopping, and...". The list goes on.

Casual

Legal High · Episode 1

そして　まんまと成功せいこうした。

"And it worked, just like that."

First the plan, then そして: it worked.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 29

それから本ほんも出だしたんだ。

"And then I also put out a book."

それから = and after that.

N5 Grammar

でも

Polite

YouTube · video

めっちゃ苦にがい。でも、苦にがさが違ちがいます。

"It's really bitter. But it's a different kind of bitter."

でも means but. It doesn't attach to anything: it stands at the start of a new sentence.

On this card, the first sentence ends (苦い。), then でも turns things around: bitter, but not the bitterness you'd expect.

Works in polite and casual speech alike. Usually followed by a small pause (でも、).

Casual

The Journalist · Episode 6

でも狭せまいぞ。

"But it's small."

でも at the start of a sentence means "but", same in polite and casual talk. On this card, 狭い = "small, cramped", and ぞ adds a rough "I'm telling you".

Examples

A friend asks about your new apartment.

駅えきから遠とおい。でも、広ひろいよ。

"It's far from the station. But it's big."

Casual

Your teacher asks if you did the homework.

はい、やりました。でも、家いえに忘わすれました。

"Yes, I did it. But I left it at home."

Polite

Someone says sushi is expensive in Japan.

でも、回転かいてん寿司すしは安やすいですよ。

"But conveyor-belt sushi is cheap."

The first sentence can come from the other person. でも pushes back on what they just said.

Polite

Your friend wants to go out, but you're tired.

行いきたい。でも、眠ねむい…

"I want to go. But I'm sleepy..."

Casual

With and without

Without

この店みせは高たかい。おいしい。

"This place is expensive. It's good." Two facts, no link.

With でも

この店みせは高たかい。でも、おいしい。

"This place is expensive. But it's good." Now the second sentence pushes back against the first.

Same "but" as けど and が (But), just in a different spot. けど and が glue onto the end of the first part (高いけど、おいしい). でも starts a fresh sentence (高い。でも、おいしい).

Sentence mining

Polite

Legal High · Episode 6

でも、無駄むだでした。

"But it was pointless."

でも ("but") + 無駄でした ("it was pointless"). でも starts a new sentence that goes against the last one.

Polite

Sailor Suit and Machine Gun · Episode 4

でも 幸しあわせです。

"But I'm happy."

でも ("but") + 幸せです ("I'm happy"). Despite everything before, she's happy.

Casual

YouTube · video

でも、さすがにもう穴掘あなほりもしたいからな。

"But I really want to do some digging now too."

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 14

でもむきむきすぎないの

"But not too muscly [okay?]"

In fast casual speech the pause after でも often disappears.

Casual

The Cat Returns

でも ムタさんは？

"But what about Muta?"

でも ("but") + ムタさんは？ ("what about Muta?"). は？ asks about someone else.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

でもどうして？

"But why?"

でも starts the new sentence.

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

N5 Grammar

が (But)

Polite

YouTube · video

元々もともとは、アパレル関係かんけいの仕事しごとをしていましたが

"Originally, I worked in fashion, but... [now I make miniatures]"

が at the end of a sentence part means but. It goes after the whole sentence, usually after です or ます: していました + が = "I did, but...".

On this card, she's setting up a contrast: that was then, and something different is coming. You can even stop right after が and leave the rest unsaid.

が is the polite "but". With friends you'd say けど instead: していたけど.

Casual

Smoking · Episode 3

残念ざんねんだが 諦あきらめてくれ

"It's a shame, but give up on it."

が can follow a plain sentence too, but it sounds stiff, so most people say けど in casual talk. On this card, 残念だ ("it's a shame") + が + 諦めてくれ ("give up") sounds stern.

Examples

A coworker asks how the new job is going.

忙いそがしいですが、楽たのしいです。

"It's busy, but it's fun."

Sentence + が + sentence. The second half goes against what the first half makes you expect.

Polite

At a shop, you ask for a size they don't have.

すみません、Mはありませんが、Lはあります。

"Sorry, we don't have M, but we have L."

ません + が works too. No M, but here's another option.

Polite

Calling a restaurant to ask about tonight.

今晩こんばんの予約よやくをしたいんですが…

"I'd like to make a reservation for tonight, but... [is that possible?]"

Stopping at が makes a request soft. The other person fills in the rest.

Polite

With and without

Without

日本にほん語ごは難むずかしいです。好すきです。

"Japanese is hard. I like it." Two separate facts, no link.

With が

日本にほん語ごは難むずかしいですが、好すきです。

"Japanese is hard, but I like it." Now the second part pushes back against the first.

Not the same as the subject marker が. That one comes right after a noun (猫がいる). This one comes after a whole sentence, usually after です or ます, and often has a comma after it.

Sentence mining

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 8

何なにか、あの、編集へんしゅう長ちょうが先さきに来きているはずなんですが

"Um, the editor-in-chief should already be here, but... [I don't see them]"

Two が here. 編集長が is the subject marker (after a noun). The one at the end, after んです, is "but", and the rest is left unsaid.

Polite

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 10

8校こう受うけましたが、

"I applied to eight schools, but..."

8校 ("eight schools") + 受けました ("applied, took the exams") + が = "I applied to eight, but...". The bad news follows.

Polite

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 10

こんなときですが、長ながい間あいだお世話せわになりました。

"It's a strange time to say it, but thank you for everything."

です + が: softens what comes next.

Polite

Boku no Hero Academia · Episode 10

ですが、何なにか変更へんこうがあったのでしょうか？

"But has something changed?"

です + が at the start = "however", the polite でも. 何か変更があった: "did something change?".

Polite

Hunter × Hunter · Episode 25

ですが、少すこし悪わるふざけが過すぎました。

"But the joke went a bit too far."

です + が at the start = "however". 悪ふざけが過ぎました: "the joke went too far".

Polite

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 2

少すこしずつですが、

"Slowly, but..."

少しずつ ("little by little") + です + が = "slowly, but...". The main point follows.

Polite

Good Morning Call · Episode 1

これなんですがね

"This is it, though…"

が at the end leaves the sentence open and softer.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 16

大盛おおもりもできますが。

"We can also make it a large [if you like]."

The sentence stops at が, leaving the offer open.

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

N5 Grammar

けど・けれども

Polite～ですけど everyday polite
～けれども careful, to an audience
Casual～けど

Same meaning: "but". けど is fine in polite speech too.

Casual

YouTube · video

ちょっと見みにくいけど、日本にほんの国旗こっきがあります。

"It's a little hard to see, but there's a Japanese flag."

けど means but. It goes right after a whole sentence part: 見にくい + けど = "it's hard to see, but...".

On this card, the second half goes against what the first half makes you expect: hard to see, but it's there.

けど is the everyday "but", fine with friends and even in polite speech (ですけど). It's the short form of けれども.

Polite

YouTube · video

色々いろいろ選択せんたく肢しがあるんですけれども、とりあえず、まあ、魚釣さかなつりから始はじめてみましょうか。

"There are lots of options, but for now, let's start with fishing."

けれども is the full, careful version of けど, in the same spot. You hear it when someone talks politely to an audience, like this YouTuber.

Examples

A friend asks about the new ramen place.

高たかいけど、おいしいよ。

"It's pricey, but it's good."

い-adjective + けど. Nothing to add in between.

Casual

Your friend invites you out tonight.

行いきたいけど、明日あした早はやいんだ。

"I want to go, but I have an early day tomorrow."

Casual

Talking about your Japanese.

日本にほん語ごは好すきだけど、文法ぶんぽうは難むずかしい。

"I like Japanese, but grammar is hard."

After a な-adjective or a noun, add だ first: 好きだけど, 学生だけど. Without だ it sounds cut off.

Casual

At a hotel desk, asking for help.

すみません、Wi-Fiが使つかえないんですけど…

"Excuse me, the Wi-Fi isn't working... [can you help?]"

Stopping at けど makes it soft. You say the problem and let the other person offer help.

Polite

With and without

Without

この部屋へやは狭せまい。安やすい。

"This room is small. It's cheap." Two facts, no link.

With けど

この部屋へやは狭せまいけど、安やすい。

"This room is small, but it's cheap." Now the second part pushes back against the first.

Same job as が (But). が sounds a bit more formal; けど works almost everywhere.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

楽たのしいんですけど、売上うりあげは下さがってきてます。

"It's fun, but sales are going down."

んです + けど: very common in polite speech. Fun job, but the numbers say otherwise.

Polite

YouTube · video

僕ぼくは豚骨とんこつラーメンも好すきなんですけど、味噌みそラーメンの方ほうが好すきです。

"I like tonkotsu ramen too, but I prefer miso ramen."

Polite

I'm Taking the Day Off · Episode 4

分わかってますけど。

"I know that."

ますけど: polite, with a "so what?" feel.

Casual

YouTube · video

そう、時間じかんを作つくるのは難むずかしいけど

"Yeah, making the time is hard, but... [it's worth it]"

The sentence stops at けど. The "but" is there, the rest is left unsaid.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 3

新あたらしいパンダグッズ、買かっちゃったんだけど

"I bought some new panda goods, so... [want to see?]"

Here けど isn't really "but". It just opens a topic and waits for a reaction. Very common at the end of a casual sentence.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 3

分わかるけど

"I get it, but..."

分かる ("understand") + けど = "I get it, but...". The "but" is left hanging.

Casual

Sword Art Online · Episode 5

ああは言いったけど

"I said that, but..."

言った ("said") + けど = "I said it, but...". ああは: "like that".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 29

おいしいけど。

"It's good [but...]."

The sentence stops at けど, the "but" is left unsaid.

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

N5 Grammar

から (Because)

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 12

雨あめちょっと強つよいから、気きをつけてな。

"The rain's a bit heavy, so be careful."

から after a sentence means because or so. It goes right after the reason: 雨ちょっと強い + から = "because the rain's a bit heavy".

The reason comes first, then what follows from it. On this card, the sentence answers "Why should I be careful?": the rain.

This one is casual. Politely you'd say 強いですから、気をつけてください.

Polite

YouTube · video

大おおきい花火はなび大会たいかいですからね。

"It's a big fireworks festival, after all."

After a noun you need です or だ before から: 花火大会 + です + から. The sentence can stop at から when the result is already clear.

Examples

You and a coworker are about to leave, and it's pouring.

雨あめですから、タクシーで行いきましょう。

"It's raining, so let's take a taxi."

Noun + です + から. Reason first, then the plan.

Polite

Back home after a long walk with a friend.

お腹なかすいたから、何なにか食たべよう。

"I'm hungry, so let's eat something."

Verbs and い-adjectives take から directly. No だ needed.

Casual

A friend asks why you didn't come yesterday.

忙いそがしかったから。

"Because I was busy."

Answering "why?" with just the reason + から. The rest is in the question.

Casual

You and a friend are looking for a place to study.

図書としょ館かんは静しずかだから、そこで勉強べんきょうしよう。

"The library is quiet, so let's study there."

な-adjectives work like nouns: 静か + だ + から. Never 静かな + から.

Casual

With and without

Without

寒さむい。窓まどを閉しめて。

"It's cold. Close the window." Two separate lines. You have to guess they're linked.

With から

寒さむいから、窓まどを閉しめて。

"It's cold, so close the window." Now the cold is clearly the reason.

Not the same as から (From). That one comes right after a place, time or person (駅から). This one comes after a whole reason, which ends in a verb, an adjective, です or だ.

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

カビが生はえてほしくないから、もう毎朝まいあさ拭ふきますよ。

"I don't want mold to grow, so I wipe it every morning."

The reason is a whole little sentence: カビが生えてほしくない. から goes after all of it.

Polite

Weakest Beast · Episode 4

あるから来きたんです。

"I came because there is one."

ある ("there is") + から + 来たんです ("I came") = "I came because there is one".

Polite

I am Mita, Your Housekeeper · Episode 8

もどかしいからです

"Because it's frustrating."

Reason + からです: answering "why?" politely.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

大丈夫だいじょうぶ、体型たいけい似にてるから。

"It's fine, [because] our body shapes are similar."

Here the result comes first (大丈夫) and the reason is added after, ending in から. Very common in speech.

Casual

Daily Lives of High School Boys · Episode 9

おごるから。

"I'll treat you."

おごる ("treat, pay for you") + から: "because I'm treating". The rest ("so come along") is left unsaid.

Casual

From Up on Poppy Hill

いいよ、済すませて来きたから。

"It's fine, I already ate."

済ませて来た ("already took care of it") + から = "because I already ate". いいよ: "it's fine".

Reference

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

Entry "kara³" (because) · pp. 179–181

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Compound Sentences · Reason or causation using 「から」 and 「ので」

N5 Grammar

ので

Polite

YouTube · video

今日きょうは平日へいじつなので、ちょっと空あいています。

"It's a weekday today, so it's not very crowded."

ので after a sentence means because or so, like から. The reason comes first: 今日は平日 + なので = "since it's a weekday".

On this card, the sentence answers "Why is it so empty?": it's a weekday. ので sounds softer than から, like explaining the situation, so it's the one you hear most in polite talk.

After a noun or a な-adjective, put な before ので: 平日なので. Never 平日だので.

Very polite

Pokémon: Indigo League · Episode 2

ポケモン誘拐ゆうかいの被害ひがいが目立めだっておりますのでご注意ちゅういください。

"Pokémon kidnappings have been on the rise, so please be careful."

In announcements and shops, ので often comes after ます or です: おります + ので. That's extra polite.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 45

みんなで釣つったので全員ぜんいんに出だすよ。

"We all caught them together, so everyone gets some."

ので gives the reason, and it works in casual talk too. On this card, the plain 釣った and the よ ending keep it casual.

Examples

You call your boss in the morning.

熱ねつがあるので、今日きょうは休やすみます。

"I have a fever, so I'll take today off."

Verbs take ので directly. A gentle way to give a reason when asking or telling someone something.

Polite

A friend suggests a walk, but you're tired after work.

今日きょうは疲つかれたので、家いえにいるね。

"I'm tired today, so I'll stay home."

ので works in casual talk too. It just sounds a bit softer than から.

Casual

At a hotel desk, the receptionist hands you a map.

駅えきは少すこし遠とおいので、バスが便利べんりですよ。

"The station is a bit far, so the bus is handy."

い-adjectives take ので directly. No な needed.

Polite

You're showing a friend your neighborhood.

この辺へんは静しずかなので、好すきなんです。

"It's quiet around here, so I like it."

な-adjectives work like nouns: 静か + な + ので.

Polite

With and without

With から

雨あめだから、行いかない。

"It's raining, so I'm not going." Direct. Fine with friends, but can sound blunt.

With ので

雨あめなので、行いきません。

"Since it's raining, I won't go." Softer, like you're explaining the situation. Note: 雨だから but 雨なので.

Same meaning as から (Because). The two differences: ので sounds softer and more polite, and after a noun or な-adjective it takes な (平日なので), where から takes だ (平日だから).

Sentence mining

Polite

YouTube · video

私わたしは結構けっこう酔よいやすいタイプなので、船酔ふなよいしないか心配しんぱいでした。

"I'm the type who gets motion sick easily, so I was worried about getting seasick."

タイプ is a noun, so it takes な: タイプ + な + ので.

Polite

YouTube · video

私わたしは目めが悪わるすぎるのでめがねのレンズがとても分厚ぶあついですね。

"My eyesight is really bad, so my glasses lenses are very thick."

The reason (bad eyes) first, then what follows from it (thick lenses).

Polite

YouTube · video

たくさん人ひとがいて、狭せまいので、ちょっと僕ぼくは苦手にがてです。

"There are lots of people and it's cramped, so I'm not great with it."

Two reasons joined with て, then ので after the second one covers both.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 46

お薬くすり出だしますので安静あんせいにして寝ねてください。

"I'll give you some medicine, so rest and get some sleep."

The doctor gives the reason first, then the instruction.

Casual

PiroPito · Minecraft #06

歩あるき回まわるともう、敵てきに追おい掛かけ回まわされて殺ころされるので。

"If you walk around, you get chased down and killed by enemies, [so I won't]."

The sentence stops at ので. The result is left unsaid because it's obvious.

Casual

YouTube · video

昨日きのうは本当ほんとうに大雨おおあめもう、雨あめがたくさん、たくさん降ふったので。

"Yesterday was really heavy rain, it rained so, so much, [so...]"

Another one trailing off at ので, very common when explaining what happened.

N5 Grammar

～前に

Polite

YouTube · video

あの〜、海外かいがい旅行りょこうに行いく前まえに、絶対ぜったいにこの場所ばしょに行いきます。

"Um, before I go on a trip abroad, I always come to this place."

前に means before. It goes right after a verb in dictionary form: 行く + 前に = "before going". With a noun, add の: 旅行の前に = "before the trip".

On this card, it answers "when do you do that?": first comes the thing you do, the 前に part is the moment it happens before.

The verb before 前に never changes, polite or casual. Only the end of the sentence does: 行きます / 行く.

Casual

YouTube · video

えっと、工事こうじを始はじめる前まえにこの現場げんばを視察しさつしておこう。

"Okay, before we start building, let's check out the site."

Same 始める + 前に, casual ending (しておこう). In casual speech the comma after 前に is often just a tiny pause, or nothing.

Examples

Your kid is heading to bed.

寝ねる前まえに歯はを磨みがいて。

"Brush your teeth before you go to bed."

Casual

Someone asks how long you studied before moving to Japan.

日本にほんに来くる前まえに、二に年ねん勉強べんきょうしました。

"I studied for two years before I came to Japan."

Even when it's all in the past, it's 来る前に, never 来た前に. The verb before 前に stays in dictionary form.

Polite

A coworker asks where you got your coffee.

会議かいぎの前まえに買かいました。

"I bought it before the meeting."

会議 is a noun, so it needs の: 会議の前に.

Polite

A friend is about to leave your place.

帰かえる前まえに、これ食たべない？

"Want to eat this before you head home?"

Casual

With and without

Without

手てを洗あらって、ご飯はんを食たべる。

"I wash my hands and eat." Two things, in the order they happen.

With 前に

ご飯はんを食たべる前まえに、手てを洗あらう。

"Before I eat, I wash my hands." Same order in real life, but now eating is the moment, and washing is what you do first.

The clip stops at 前に, so you hear the pattern on its own. He goes on to say what to do first.

Casual

"Before dinner..."

ご飯 ("a meal, dinner") + の + 前に = "before dinner". Nouns need の before 前に.

Casual

Dictionary form + 前に, even when the story is in the past.

Casual

鬼おにが来くる前まえに隠かくれなきゃ！

"We have to hide before he comes!"

来る ("come") + 前に = "before he comes". 隠れなきゃ: "we have to hide".

Casual

Border · Episode 3

うちに来くる前まえに

"Before coming to us..."

うち ("our place") + に + 来る ("come") + 前に = "before coming to us".

Casual

Bunny Drop · Episode 3

寝ねる前まえにトイレ行いっとけば大丈夫だいじょうぶ。

"If you go to the bathroom before bed, you'll be fine."

寝る ("sleep") + 前に = "before bed". トイレ行っとけば: "if you go to the bathroom (in advance)".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 36

寝ねる前まえに嫌いやなこと言いうんじゃねえよ。

"Don't say nasty stuff right before bed."

Dictionary form + 前に.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 29

つける前まえに気きづいてよ。

"Notice that before you stick them on."

Dictionary form + 前に, even when the action is past.

Entry "mae ni" · pp. 231–233

N5 Grammar

～た後で

後で means after. Put it after the past form of a verb: 食べた + 後で = after eating. Always the past form, even when you talk about later.

With a noun, add の: 仕事の後で (after work). The politeness comes from the end of the sentence.

Close to てから: both mean "after". てから puts the focus on "first this, then that"; 後で is just "at some point after".

Examples

A friend wants to call you.

晩ばんご飯はんを食たべた後あとで電話でんわするね。

"I'll call you after dinner."

食べる → 食べた + 後で. Past form, even for later tonight.

Casual

The doctor explains your medicine.

この薬くすりは、ご飯はんの後あとで飲のんでください。

"Please take this medicine after meals."

With a noun: noun + の + 後で.

Polite

Telling a coworker about yesterday.

仕事しごとが終おわった後あとで、ジムに行いきました。

"After work, I went to the gym."

Polite

Your kid wants to play a game.

お風呂ふろに入はいった後あとでね。

"After your bath, okay?"

Casual

With and without

Without

映画えいがを見みました。ご飯はんを食たべました。

"I watched a movie. I ate." The order isn't clear.

With 後で

映画えいがを見みた後あとで、ご飯はんを食たべました。

"After the movie, I ate." Now the order is clear.

"After the picnic, I'm treating my friend to ice cream."

Noun + の後で.

Polite

もうね、他たの人ひとと日本にほん語ごで喋しゃべり終おわった後あとなんですが、この動画どうがを撮とってます。

"But that's for after the battle is over."

終わった ("ended") + 後 = "after it ended". 戦いが: "the battle". の話: "a story for".

Polite

この絵えは描えがき終おえた後あと、どうするんですか？

"What will you do with this painting after it's done?"

描き終えた ("finished painting") + 後 = "after it's finished". Past form, even for the future.

子供こどもたちが、うんと遊あそんだ後あとに休やすんでいる。

"The kids are resting after playing hard."

後に works like 後で.

爪つめを切きったあと エタノールで拭ふいたのよ。

"After cutting the nails, she wiped them with ethanol."

切った ("cut") + あと = "after cutting". Then エタノールで拭いた: "wiped them with ethanol".

"After the church ceremony..."

式挙げた ("held the ceremony") + あと = "after the ceremony". 教会で: "at a church".

"One day, after catching lots of salmon in the river [I took a nap]."

N5 Grammar

～とき (時)

Polite

NHK やさしいことばニュース · 暑い日が続く　熱中症に気をつけて

たくさん汗あせが出でたときは、塩分えんぶんをとってください。

"When you've sweated a lot, have some salt." [hot weather advice]

とき means when: it marks the moment something else happens. 汗が出たとき = when you've sweated.

Put it after a plain verb, like a noun with a description: 出た + とき. On this card, it answers "When should I have salt?": when you've sweated a lot.

With a noun, add の: 子供のとき (when I was a kid). With a な-adjective, な: 暇なとき. Politeness only shows at the end of the sentence.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 4

そういう時ときもあるね。

"There are times like that."

時 works like a noun, so it can take particles like も. On this card, そういう時 ("times like that") + も + ある = "there are times like that".

Examples

Telling a friend about growing up.

子供こどものとき、よく川かわで遊あそんだ。

"When I was a kid, I often played in the river."

Noun + の + とき.

Casual

Getting to know a coworker.

暇ひまなときは、何なにをしますか。

"What do you do when you have free time?"

な-adjective + な + とき.

Polite

Your mom reminds you.

寝ねるとき、電気でんきを消けしてね。

"Turn off the light when you go to bed."

Dictionary form: right as it happens.

Casual

Talking about a trip.

日本にほんに行いったとき、富士ふじ山やまを見みました。

"When I went to Japan, I saw Mt. Fuji."

Past form: it already happened.

Polite

With and without

Without

雨あめが降ふります。家いえにいます。

"It rains. I stay home." Two separate facts.

With とき

雨あめが降ふるときは、家いえにいます。

"When it rains, I stay home." The first part says when.

Entry "toki" · pp. 490–494

N5 Grammar

～たり～たりする

Polite

YouTube · video

観光かんこう地ちに行いったり、温泉おんせんに行いったりしました。

"We went sightseeing, went to hot springs, that kind of thing."

たり～たりする lists actions as examples: "things like A and B". There was more, these are just a few.

Take the past form and add り: 行った → 行ったり. Then end with する, which carries the tense and the politeness: しました. On this card, it answers "What did you do?": sightseeing, hot springs, stuff like that.

Compare て: 行って、行きました lists everything, in order. たり just picks a few examples.

Casual

Overprotected Kahoko · Episode 10

ケーキが壊こわれたり

"The cake got broken and stuff…"

たり gives one example of what happened, with more left unsaid. On this card, 壊れた ("got broken") + り = "got broken and stuff".

Examples

A coworker asks about your weekend.

週末しゅうまつは、本ほんを読よんだり、映画えいがを見みたりしました。

"On the weekend I read, watched movies, that sort of thing."

読んだ → 読んだり. 見た → 見たり.

Polite

A friend asks what you do on the train.

音楽おんがくを聞きいたり、寝ねたりしてる。

"I listen to music, sleep, stuff like that."

してる = している, casual.

Casual

Talking about the weather.

最近さいきん、雨あめが降ふったり止やんだりしています。

"Lately it keeps raining on and off."

Two opposites: back and forth.

Polite

Someone asks about your days off.

休やすみの日ひは、料理りょうりをしたりする。

"On my days off I do stuff like cooking."

One たり is fine too: "things like cooking".

Casual

With and without

Without

本ほんを読よんで、映画えいがを見みました。

"I read a book, then watched a movie." That's what I did, in order.

With たり

本ほんを読よんだり、映画えいがを見みたりしました。

"I read, watched movies, that kind of thing." Just examples, there was more.

"After that I walked around and looked at things, killing time."

おむつを変かえたり、ミルクを飲のませたり、いろいろお世話せわしないといけないです。

N5 Grammar

～の

Polite～んですか
Casual～の？

Same meaning: asking for the story. Only the politeness changes.

Casual

Source unknown

このジャグ　どうしたの？

"Where did this dispenser come from?"

の at the end of a question asks for the story behind something you noticed. It goes after a verb or adjective in plain form (after nouns and な-adjectives, add な: 学生なの？).

On this card, they spot a drink dispenser that wasn't there before. Literally "this jug, what happened?". It asks "What's the story here?".

This is casual. Polite: どうしたんですか？ Without の, どうした？ sounds blunter, just "what happened?".

Polite

Source unknown

え、ここで申請しんせいできるんですか？

"Huh, can I apply here?"

Here it's ん instead of の, plus ですか: you noticed something surprising and want the story. Use it with strangers, staff and clients.

Examples

Your friend walks in wearing flip-flops, a towel over their shoulder, a bag of snacks.

海うみ行いくの？

"Oh, you're going to the beach?"

Saw something

Dinner's been on the table for 20 minutes. Your friend hasn't touched their plate.

食たべないの？

"You're not eating? Everything okay?"

Saw something

Over coffee, your friend casually says 「昨日、仕事辞めた」.

辞やめたの？

"Wait, you quit? What happened?"

Heard something

A client's sweater is covered in cat hair.

家いえに猫ねこがいるんですか？

"Oh, do you have a cat?"

Saw something

With and without

Without

海うみ行いく？

"Wanna go to the beach?" Out of nowhere, you're bored.

With の

海うみ行いくの？

"Oh, you're going to the beach?" You saw the towel.

Without

食たべない？

"Want some?" Offering your pizza.

With の

食たべないの？

"You're not eating?" You saw the full plate.

Polite: んですか

Same feeling, just polite. ん is a squashed の. More about ～んです

Casual

猫ねこいるの？

To a friend.

Polite

猫ねこがいるんですか？

To a client.

Written: のですか

The full form is の + ですか = のですか. Said quickly, the の gets squashed into ん, so you get んですか. Same meaning, both correct. In conversation it's almost always んですか. のですか is for books and articles, and said out loud it sounds stiff, like a news reader.

Spoken

猫ねこがいるんですか？

What you'll hear and say.

Written

猫ねこがいるのですか？

Books, articles, very formal speech.

When to add な

Noun or な-adjective right before の? Put な in between. Verbs and い-adjectives get nothing.

Your friend shows up soaked, no umbrella.

雨あめなの？

"Oh, is it raining?"

Casual
Verb / い-adjective

行いくの？　高たかいの？

Nothing added.

Noun / な-adjective

雨あめなの？　好すきなの？

Add な.

へぇ～　今日きょうは折おり紙がみ折おらないんですか？

"Oh, you're not doing origami today?"

They usually fold origami, but today they aren't. You noticed, so you ask. The へぇ～ is a hint too: it's the sound of reacting to something.

"What's this? Is this an underwater cave?"

You're looking at something strange and asking what's going on. 洞窟 is a noun, so な goes before の.

"Wait, you ate it?!"

The food is gone, she noticed, and she wants the story. 食べちゃった is a casual 食べてしまった: ate it all up.

"You got picked as class rep? Wow."

Just heard the news and wants the story. Past verb + の, rising voice.

"You met him?"

会った ("met") + の with a rising voice = "you met him?". Wanting to hear more.

Casual

どんな人 ("what kind of person") + な + の = "what's she like?". Nouns take な before の.

"Aren't you feeling well?"

具合が悪い ("feel unwell") + の = "aren't you feeling well?". She sees something's off and asks.

A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

Entry "no⁴" (sentence-final particle) · pp. 322–324

Tae Kim's Guide to Japanese Grammar

Noun-related Particles · The 「の」 particle as explanation

N5 Grammar

～んです・のです

Polite～んです spoken
～のです formal, written
Casual～んだ

Same meaning: giving the reason or story. Only the politeness changes.

Polite

He Who Can't Marry · Episode 1

だから１階かい建だてなんです！

"That's why it's a single-story building!"

んです adds "here's the reason or the story behind it". It goes after a verb or adjective in plain form. After a noun or な-adjective, add な: １階建て + な + んです.

On this card, he's explained the background, and this is the conclusion. だから is "that's why", and なんです marks the whole thing as an explanation. It answers "Why is it like that?". Without it, １階建てです is just a plain fact.

This is polite. Casual: １階建てなんだ. In writing: １階建てなのです.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Season 1, Episode 2

これ試ためしに作つくってみたんだ。

"[You see,] I tried making this."

He shows what he made and gives the story behind it. んだ is what you'd use with friends and family.

Examples

You show up late. Your friend gives you a look.

電車でんしゃが遅おくれたんです。

"The train was late, that's why."

Explaining

You're carrying a box of art supplies, way behind your friend. They turn around like "come on!"

重おもいんです！

"It's heavy, okay!"

Explaining

A client keeps pointing at the red cover option.

赤あかがいいんですか？

"Oh, so you want red?" (asking about something you noticed)

Asking

A friend offers you the last piece of cake.

いいんですか？

"Are you sure? Is that really okay?"

With いいですか？ you're asking for permission. With いいんですか？ you're reacting to something.

Asking

You show a friend your illustration. They laugh: "no way, you didn't draw that, you used AI."

本当ほんとうに描えがいたんです！

"I really did draw it!" You're pushing back on what they think.

Pushing back

You come back from the beach and tell a friend what you saw.

富士ふじ山やまがすごくきれいだったんです！

"Mt. Fuji was SO beautiful!" Sharing a feeling and pulling them into it.

Sharing a feeling

With and without

Without

重おもいです。

Just a fact. Someone asks how heavy the box is, you report it.

With んです

重おもいんです。

The reason for what's going on. That's why I'm slow.

Without

赤あかがいいですか？

Neutral offer, out of nowhere. A waiter asking "red or white?"

With んです

赤あかがいいんですか？

You noticed something and you're checking. Can sound a bit surprised.

Without

描えがきました。

"I drew it." Just reporting.

With んです

描えがいたんです！

"I DID draw it!" Insisting, because you're reacting to something in the air (their doubt).

Casual: んだ and の

Same thing, just casual. In games, anime and with friends you'll hear these far more than んです. の works in statements too, not just questions: it's a softer んだ.

You show up late to meet a friend.

電車でんしゃが遅おくれたんだ。

"The train was late, that's why."

Casual

Your friend looks upset.

どうしたの？

"What happened?"

Casual

A friend asks why you left your food.

お腹なかすいてないの。

"I'm just not hungry, that's all."

の as a statement sounds soft and can sound a bit feminine. Guys more often say んだ: お腹すいてないんだ. Often followed by ね or よ: すごいのね.

Casual
Polite

遅おくれたんです。

To a client or a stranger.

Casual

遅おくれたんだ。

To a friend.

Polite

どうしたんですか？

To a client or a stranger.

Casual

どうしたの？

To a friend.

Written: のです

Same thing in its full form. You'll see it in books and articles. In conversation it can sound a bit stiff.

Spoken

遅おくれたんです。

What you'll hear almost always.

Written

遅おくれたのです。

Books, articles, formal writing.

When to add な

With nouns and な-adjectives, add な. Verbs and い-adjectives get nothing. More about な

A friend asks why you never order ramen.

ラーメンが嫌きらいなんです。

"I don't like ramen, that's why."

Polite
Verb / い-adjective

遅おくれたんです

Nothing added.

Noun / な-adjective

嫌きらいなんです

Add な.

N5 Grammar

のは・のが

Polite

Source unknown

昼間ひるまに山道さんどうを歩あるくのは楽たのしいです

"Walking along the mountain path during the day is fun."

の turns an action into a thing. 歩く "walk" → 歩くの "walking" (as in "walking is fun", not "I'm walking").

On this card, the whole shaded chunk 昼間に山道を歩く becomes one thing, and は makes it the topic: "walking the mountain path in the daytime" is fun.

のが works the same way: 歩くのが好き, "I like walking".

Casual

YouTube · video

今日きょう行いくのは、逗子ずしという街まちだ。

"Where I'm going today is a town called Zushi."

のは turns a verb into "the place or thing that...", and the answer comes last. On this card, 今日行くのは = "the place I'm going today", and casual だ ends it.

Examples

A friend asks what you do on weekends. You love swimming.

泳およぐのが好すき。

"I like swimming."

の works like English "-ing": swim becomes swimming.

の = the act

Your alarm goes off at 5am, it's dark and cold.

朝あさ早はやく起おきるのはつらい。

"Getting up early is rough."

The whole chunk 朝早く起きる becomes one thing, then は: as for that, it's rough.

の = the act

At a party, someone asks who made the cake.

ケーキを作つくったのは母ははだ。

"The one who made the cake is my mom."

Everyone knows someone made it. The answer comes last, like a reveal.

の = the one

Back from a trip to Japan, a friend asks about the food.

一番いちばんおいしかったのはラーメンだった。

"The thing that was tastiest was the ramen."

の = the thing

With and without

Not this

泳およぐが好すき。

Broken. Like "I like swim". が needs a thing, and 泳ぐ is an action.

With の

泳およぐのが好すき。

"I like swimming." の turns the action into a thing.

Without

母ははがケーキを作つくった。

"Mom made the cake." Just the plain fact.

With の

ケーキを作つくったのは母ははだ。

"The one who made the cake? Mom." Same fact, but the answer is saved for the end.

When to add な

Noun or な-adjective right before の? Put な in between. Verbs and い-adjectives get nothing.

Verb / い-adjective

泳およぐのが好すき。　寒さむいのが苦手にがて。

Nothing added.

Noun / な-adjective

静しずかなのがいい。

"Quiet is good." Add な.

More on the particles themselves: は and が.

N4 Grammar

とか

Polite

YouTube · video

日本にほんには、焼やき肉にくとか、鍋なべとかがあります。

"In Japan there are things like yakiniku and nabe."

とか lists examples: "A, B, things like that". It tells the listener there's more, you're only naming a few.

It goes after each item (A とか B とか), and the particle comes after the last one. On this card, yakiniku and nabe are two examples of Japanese food, and there are plenty of others.

とか itself doesn't change between polite and casual. It's a spoken word: in writing you'll see や instead.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 19

特別とくべつ快速かいそくとか、通勤つうきん急行きゅうこうとか、いろいろありすぎ。

"Special Rapid, Commuter Express... there are way too many [kinds of train]."

On this card, two train types are just examples, and いろいろ ("all sorts") right after says there are lots more.

Examples

A friend asks what you do on weekends.

映画えいがとか、ゲームとか。

"Movies, games, that kind of thing."

Casual

A waiter checks before taking your order.

卵たまごとか、食たべられないものはありますか？

"Is there anything you can't eat, like eggs?"

Eggs are just one example of what they mean.

Polite

Your friend looks tired.

コーヒーとか飲のむ？

"Want a coffee or something?"

One とか on its own: "or something". Softer than just コーヒー飲む？

Casual

With and without

With と

テニスとサッカーをしました。

"I played tennis and soccer." That's the full list.

With とか

テニスとかサッカーとかをしました。

"I played tennis, soccer, stuff like that." Those are examples, there was more.

N4 Grammar

Particle + の

Noun + particle + の + Noun

A particle normally hangs on a verb. Add の and it can hang on a noun instead, keeping its meaning.

友達との約束 = "a promise with a friend"
日本での生活 = "life in Japan"
母からの手紙 = "a letter from my mom"
東京への旅 = "a trip to Tokyo"
駅までの道 = "the way to the station"

Polite

YouTube · video

やっぱり、この人ひとと人ひととの交流こうりゅうですね。

"In the end, it's the connection between people, isn't it?"

との is と ("with") + の. A particle can't sit right in front of a noun, so の is added to hook it on.

The particle keeps its meaning: と still says who with whom, の just lets it describe the noun after it.

On this card, 人と人との交流 is "the connection between person and person".

Casual

Slam Dunk · Episode 86

俺おれには 父親ちちおやとの約束やくそくがある。

"I have a promise with my father."

On this card, he promised his dad he'd join the family business. 父親の約束 would be "my dad's promise", one his dad made; 父親との約束 is a promise the two made together.

Examples

You're telling a friend about your weekend.

彼女かのじょとのデート、楽たのしかった。

"The date with my girlfriend was fun."

Casual

A coworker asks how you like living abroad.

日本にほんでの生活せいかつは楽たのしいです。

"Life in Japan is fun."

日本で生活する = "live in Japan" (verb). 日本での生活 = "life in Japan" (noun).

Polite

Your roommate hands you an envelope.

お母かあさんからの手紙てがみだよ。

"It's a letter from your mom."

Casual

At a bookshop, picking a gift.

田中たなかさんへのプレゼントです。

"It's a present for Tanaka."

へ ("toward") + の: a present going to Tanaka.

Polite

With and without

With の only

山田やまださんの約束やくそく

"Yamada's promise." A promise Yamada made, to anyone.

With との

山田やまださんとの約束やくそく

"The promise with Yamada." A promise you made together with Yamada.

N4 Grammar

かな

Polite～でしょうか a different word, same "I wonder"
～かなと思います かな tucked inside, "I'm thinking maybe..."
Casual～かな

かな on its own is always casual. To sound polite, swap it for でしょうか, or keep it and end with と思います.

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 39

ゆずこしょう どこだったかな

"Where was the yuzu pepper again?"

かな means "I wonder". You're thinking out loud, half to yourself, and nobody has to answer.

It goes at the end of a casual sentence: a verb, an adjective or a noun (どこだった + かな, セイウチかな). On this card, he's looking around the kitchen and asking himself where the yuzu pepper is.

It's casual. In polite speech you'd say でしょうか instead. With ～てくれるかな or ～てもいいかな it becomes a soft request: "could you...?"

Examples

Looking out the window in the morning.

今日きょうは雨あめかな。

"Will it rain today, I wonder."

After a noun, no だ.

Casual

At the menu, deciding.

カレーにしようかな。

"Maybe I'll go with curry."

～ようかな: deciding out loud, "maybe I'll...".

Casual

Asking a friend for a small favor.

ちょっと手伝てつだってくれるかな？

"Could you help me a bit?"

A soft way to ask.

Casual

With and without

With か

彼かれは来くるか？

Is he coming? A real question, you want an answer.

With かな

彼かれは来くるかな。

I wonder if he's coming. Just thinking out loud.

N4 Grammar

はず

Polite～はずです
Casual～はずだ・～はず

Same meaning: "should be, I expect". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 7

適切てきせつな対応たいおうをしてくれるはずです。

"They should handle it properly."

はず means "should be": you expect it, because of what you know. It's your reasoning, not a promise.

It goes after a verb or adjective as is (くれる + はず), after a noun with の (休みのはず), after a な-adjective with な. On this card, the speaker trusts them to deal with it properly: that's what you'd expect from them.

In English it's often "should", but it never means "you should do it" (advice). That's a different word.

Casual

Kekkon Dekinai Otoko · Episode 5

たぶん この中なかにあるはずだ

"It should be in here, probably."

On this card, he's looking for something and reasons it out: it has to be in here. Casual drops です; it can end on はず alone too.

Examples

Your friend's train left an hour ago.

彼かれはもう着ついたはずだよ。

"He should have arrived by now."

You worked it out from the time.

Casual

A coworker asks if the meeting is on Monday.

月曜日げつようびのはずです。

"It should be on Monday."

After a noun, add の.

Polite

Someone says your shy friend went to a party.

そんなはずない！

"No way, that can't be!"

はずない (or はずがない): "it can't be".

Casual

With and without

Without

彼かれは来くる。

He's coming. You know it for sure.

With はず

彼かれは来くるはずだ。

He should be coming. That's what you expect, from what you know.

N4 Grammar

みたい

Polite～みたいです
Casual～みたいだ・～みたい

Same meaning: "seems like". Only the politeness changes.

Polite

YouTube · video

行いき方かたが分わかったみたいです。

"Looks like she's figured out the way."

みたい means "seems like, looks like": you're saying what it looks like from what you see or hear, without being sure.

It goes straight after a verb, an adjective or a noun (分かった + みたい, 雨みたい). On this card, he watches someone and guesses from how they act that they now know the way.

After a noun it can also mean "like" (a comparison): 夢みたい, "like a dream".

Casual

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 19

ああ まぁ エゾリスたちとは 打うち解とけたみたいだな

"Yeah, well, looks like he's warmed up to the squirrels."

On this card, he guesses from what he sees: they seem to get along now. Casual drops です; みたいだな adds a thinking-out-loud feel.

Examples

You look out the window, the street is wet.

雨あめが降ふったみたい。

"Looks like it rained."

You didn't see it rain, the street tells you.

Casual

A colleague's desk has been empty all day.

田中たなかさんは休やすみみたいです。

"Looks like Tanaka is off today."

After a noun, no の or な: 休みみたい.

Polite

You taste a homemade dish.

お店みせみたいな味あじだね！

"It tastes like a restaurant!"

みたいな + noun: "a ... like ...".

Casual

With and without

Without

田中たなかさんは休やすみです。

Tanaka is off. You know it.

With みたい

田中たなかさんは休やすみみたいです。

Tanaka seems to be off. That's how it looks, you're not sure.
