N4 Grammar

のに

Polite

Kekkon Dekinai Otoko · Episode 6

断ことわってるのに しつこく メールしてくるんですよ

"I keep turning them down, and yet they keep emailing me."

のに means "even though": A, and yet B. B isn't what you'd expect after A, and usually you're annoyed, disappointed or surprised about it.

It goes after a verb or い-adjective as is (断ってる + のに), after a noun or な-adjective with な (雨なのに). On this card, saying no should stop the emails, and yet they keep coming. The speaker is fed up.

The politeness comes from the end of the sentence, のに itself never changes.

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 7

寒さむいのに 待またせちゃってごめんね。

"Sorry for making you wait when it's so cold."

On this card, it's cold, and yet he had to wait outside. She feels bad about it.

Examples

You studied all week, and still failed.

勉強べんきょうしたのに、落おちた。

"I studied, and I still failed."

You expected to pass. The のに shows the frustration.

Casual

It's Sunday, but your boss calls.

日曜日にちようびなのに、仕事しごとの電話でんわが来きました。

"It's Sunday, and yet I got a work call."

After a noun, add な.

Polite

Your friend didn't tell you about the party.

言いってくれれば行いったのに。

"If you'd told me, I would have gone."

At the end of a sentence, のに is pure regret: "and now it's too late".

Casual

With and without

With けど

勉強べんきょうしたけど、落おちた。

I studied, but I failed. Just a plain fact.

With のに

勉強べんきょうしたのに、落おちた。

I studied, and still failed! It feels unfair.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 5

パフェなのに　とってもヘルシーなんです

"It's a parfait, and yet it's really healthy."

Here the surprise is a happy one. Noun + な + のに.

Polite

Shirokuma Cafe · Episode 45

冬眠とうみん中ちゅうなのに車くるま出だしてくださって ありがとうございます

"Thank you for driving us even though you're hibernating."

He should be asleep, and yet he drove them. Thanks with a bit of guilt.

Casual

The Wind Rises

はるばる訪たずねてきたのに 工場こうじょうは立たち入いり禁止きんしだとよ

"We came all this way, and they say the factory is off limits."

All that travel, and they can't even get in.

Casual

PiroPito · First Playthrough of Minecraft #03

あれ待まって、朝あさなのに蜘蛛くもがいる。

"Wait, it's morning, and there's a spider?"

Spiders should be gone by morning. Noun + な + のに.

Casual

Slam Dunk · Episode 99

2万まん本ぼんも練習れんしゅうしたのによ おかしいじゃねえか

"I practiced 20,000 shots, and yet... that's not right!"

All that practice should have paid off.

Casual

1 Litre of Tears · Episode 3

夜よる遅おそくなるまで練習れんしゅうしたのに。

"Even though I practiced until late at night."

The second half is left unsaid: it didn't work out.

Casual

Kotaro Lives Alone · Episode 2

それならウチのシャワー 貸かしたのにな…

"If that's the case, I'd have lent you my shower."

のに at the end: regret, "if only I'd known".

Non-JLPT Grammar

ぞ

Casual

Devilman Crybaby · Episode 2

本物ほんものの銃じゅうだぞ！

"This is a real gun!"

ぞ is like よ, but much stronger: "I'm telling you!" It pushes the point at the listener, or psyches yourself up.

It goes at the very end of a casual sentence (だ + ぞ, 行く + ぞ). On this card, he wants them to take it seriously: it's a real gun.

It sounds rough and masculine, so men use it with friends, family or people below them. Never in polite speech, and the JLPT lists leave it out.

Examples

Leaving the house with your kids.

行いくぞ！

"Let's go!" / "I'm going!"

The classic one. Telling everyone it's time.

Casual

Warning a friend who's on his phone at the crossing.

危あぶないぞ！

"Watch out!"

A warning with force.

Casual

Before a big exam, to yourself.

頑張がんばるぞ！

"I'm going to do this!"

Psyching yourself up.

Casual

With and without

With よ

遅刻ちこくするよ。

You'll be late, you know. A friendly heads-up.

With ぞ

遅刻ちこくするぞ。

You'll be late! Stronger, almost an order to hurry.

Hiragana Chart

What is hiragana?

Hiragana is the basic Japanese alphabet. Each character is one sound: か is ka, き is ki. Japanese mixes three scripts in one sentence, and hiragana is the glue that holds the kanji together.

Grammar
Particles and the endings of verbs and adjectives. The kanji carries the meaning, hiragana does the grammar.本を読みました · I read a book
Words
Everyday words that are usually written without kanji.ありがとう · thank you
Readings
Small hiragana over a kanji show how to read it. That's called furigana.山 → やま · mountain
Basic46 sounds
゛ and ゜25 sounds
Combos33 sounds

Katakana Chart

What is katakana?

Katakana is the second Japanese alphabet. It has the same sounds as hiragana, just other shapes: か and カ are both ka. The shapes are sharp and straight, made from small pieces of kanji.

Loanwords
Words taken from other languages, mostly English.コーヒー · coffee
Names
Foreign names, countries and cities.アメリカ · America
Emphasis
Sound words and words that should stand out, a bit like italics.ドキドキ · heart pounding

ー makes the sound before it longer: コーヒー is koohii.

N5 Kanji

Two kinds of reading

Most kanji can be read in more than one way. Japan took kanji from China, so each kanji kept a Chinese sound, and Japan also gave it its own Japanese word with the same meaning.

On'yomi
The Chinese sound. Written in katakana in dictionaries. You hear it mostly when two or more kanji make one word.富士山 ふじさん · Mount Fuji
Kun'yomi
The Japanese word. Written in hiragana. You hear it mostly when the kanji stands alone or has hiragana after it.山 やま · mountain

Same kanji, same meaning, different sound. It's a rule of thumb: 本 alone is ほん (on), and 手紙 てがみ (letter) uses kun in a two-kanji word.

Resources

VocabularyLearn words

SRS app

  • AnkiWinMacMy SRS app of choice: flashcards that come back right before you'd forget them.
  • AnkiMobileiOSThe official Anki app for iPhone and iPad, paid, and it syncs with the desktop app.
  • AnkiDroidAndroidThe free Anki app for Android phones and tablets, and it syncs with the desktop app.

Anki decks

  • 耳Japanese course based on Tae Kim's grammar guide & animeN5N4Jlab's beginner course from zero, following Tae Kim's guide with one new word or grammar point per anime clip.
  • 単Kaishi 1.5k: Basic Japanese VocabularyA slimmed down version of the 2k/6k deck.

Dictionaries

  • JishoWebFree online Japanese-English dictionary you can search in English, Japanese or romaji.
  • Shirabe JishoiPhoneFree offline Japanese dictionary for iPhone and iPad, where you can draw a kanji to look it up.

Sentence search

  • YouGlishType a word and hear it in real YouTube clips, handy for finding sentences to mine.
  • Immersion KitSearch anime, drama and game subtitles and get each line with a screenshot and audio, ready to send to Anki.

Browser extensions

  • MigakuPaid Chrome extension that turns sites like YouTube and Netflix into study material, so you can look up words and mine them as you watch.

JLPT

Next test

The next one is 6 December 2026, but sign-up for it has most likely closed by now. So the realistic next one is July 2027. Its date isn't announced yet: going by past years it should be Sunday 4 July, with sign-up around March or April. Checked 4 Nov 2026, so check again on the official site.

What it is

The official Japanese test, run by the Japan Foundation and JEES, in Japan and many other countries. There are five levels: N5 is the easiest, N1 the hardest.

  • Only reading and listening. It's a multiple choice answer sheet with no speaking or writing. Most questions have four choices, some listening ones have three.
  • You pick your level. The official site doesn't ask for a lower level first, it just says to choose one that suits you. There's no age limit.
  • The certificate never expires, though a company or school can set its own limit.
The levels
ReadingListening
N5Typical sentences in hiragana, katakana and basic kanjiPick out what you need from short, slow conversations
N4Short passages on everyday topics, in basic words and kanjiMostly follow everyday conversations, if they're fairly slow
N3Everyday texts with specific content, and newspaper headlinesEveryday conversations at near-natural speed
N2Clear articles, commentaries and simple critiques on many topicsConversations and news at nearly natural speed
N1Complex or abstract writing, like editorials, and the writer's intentConversations, news and lectures at natural speed

N5 and N4 mainly test basic Japanese learned in class. N3 is the bridge up to N2 and N1.

The test
VocabGrammar, readingListeningTotal
N520 min40 min30 min90 min
N425 min55 min35 min115 min
N330 min70 min40 min140 min
N2105 min for all three50 min155 min
N1110 min for all three55 min165 min

Times can change a little, listening especially.

On N2 and N1, vocabulary, grammar and reading are one part with one timer, and you choose how long to spend on each. On N5, N4 and N3, vocabulary is a separate part with its own timer.

You always take every part: you can't retake only the part you failed, and missing a part means you fail.

Passing

You need two things: enough points in total, and the minimum in every score. The scores are split differently on the lower levels.

Total, out of 180Minimum in each score
N580Vocabulary, grammar and reading: 38 of 120
Listening: 19 of 60
N490Vocabulary, grammar and reading: 38 of 120
Listening: 19 of 60
N395Vocabulary and grammar, reading, listening: 19 of 60 each
N290Vocabulary and grammar, reading, listening: 19 of 60 each
N1100Vocabulary and grammar, reading, listening: 19 of 60 each

So 100 points in total with 15 for listening is a fail, on every level. Scores are scaled, not a count of right answers, so there's no fixed number of correct answers that passes.

What to study

The JLPT hasn't published official lists since 2010, so every number here is an estimate. The ones you'll see most:

WordsKanji
N5about 800about 100
N4about 1,500about 300
N3about 3,750about 650
N2about 6,000about 1,000
N1about 10,000about 2,000

Each number includes the levels below it, and N1's word count varies the most between sources.

A simple order:

  1. See the format first. Try the official sample questions: N5, N4, N3, N2, N1.
  2. Learn the material. On this site: N5 grammar, the N5 vocabulary list and the N5 kanji.
  3. Listen every week. It has its own minimum score, so strong reading can't make up for weak listening.
  4. Do timed practice. Near the test, use the Official Practice Workbook with a clock running.
Dates and deadlines

The test is twice a year, on a Sunday in July and December. Some cities outside Japan only hold one of them.

July testDecember test
Sign upabout March to Aprilabout August to September
Voucher arrivesearly Julyearly December
Test in 20265 July6 December
Results, in Japanearly Septemberearly February
Results, abroadearly Octoberearly March

Sign-up months are a rough guide, because every test city sets its own deadline and fee.

Signing up: outside Japan, find your city and its local organizer in the official list of test cities, then follow their instructions and pay them. In Japan, it goes through the Japan sign-up page.

Results: everyone gets a score report, and if you pass, a certificate too.

Support

Everything on this site is free, and it will stay that way. No ads, no sign-up, no paywall.

I build it in my free time, one grammar point at a time, while learning Japanese myself. If it has helped you and you'd like to give something back, any support is much appreciated. It helps keep the site running and growing.

And if you can't or don't want to, that's completely fine. I'm just happy it's useful to you.
